Trump Vows Unprecedented Economic Measures Against Iran Amid Stalled Talks

President Donald Trump announced on Wednesday that the United States is launching a new economic campaign against Iran, calling it "the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY." The move comes after a 60-day ceasefire expired without a diplomatic resolution to the war that began in late February. Trump warned that any country aiding Iran financially would face "TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences," though he did not specify the measures. The administration has been applying economic pressure on Iran since April, aiming to cut off its revenue streams and isolate the country. The U.S. has also imposed a naval blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, a critical oil route, which has significantly impacted Iran's economy.

The economic measures are part of a broader strategy to weaken Iran's ability to sustain its military and economic operations. Reports indicate that Iran's oil production has dropped by nearly 23 percent since the start of the conflict, reducing its ability to generate foreign currency. The U.S. and its allies are seeking to maintain control over the Strait of Hormuz, which is vital for global oil trade. Trump claimed the U.S. has "complete control" of the strait, despite Iran's continued efforts to restrict maritime traffic through the region.

Where the accounts differ

Newsweek reports that Trump's economic measures are part of "Operation Economic Fury," which includes targeting oil smuggling, swap lines, and front companies. The Daily Wire adds that Trump's actions are aimed at dismantling Iran's "shadow economy," including illicit financial networks in China, Dubai, and Malaysia. BBC notes that the UAE has severed financial ties with Iran following a missile threat, while UPI mentions that China has been a major buyer of Iranian oil and has opposed U.S. sanctions. Washington Examiner highlights the financial impact of the naval blockade, estimating it could cost Iran $18 billion annually if continued.

Sources Newsweek · BBC · UPI · Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · Axios

South Korea Wants Its Military Back

On August 27, 2025, ROK Army 7th Corps Engineer Brigade and U.S. Army 11th Engineer Battalion of the 2nd Infantry Division soldiers participated in a joint bridging drill in Yeoju, South Korea. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung reiterated calls for the country to regain full control of its military operations from the U.S. following Donald Trump’s order to cut back on annual joint training drills in preparation for North Korean threats. Trump cited his "very good relationship with Kim Jong Un" and South Korea’s refusal to support the U.S. war effort in Iran as reasons for reducing the drills. Lee responded by urging Seoul to plan a transfer of control over the Combined Forces Command, which oversees both South Korean and U.S. forces during wartime. South Korea has sought to regain wartime operational control since the 1950s Korean War, with regaining control seen as a key goal of Lee’s administration. Lee also signaled rearmament, including accelerating the development of nuclear-powered submarines.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and ABC News both mention Trump’s claim that South Korea refused to support the U.S. war effort in Iran, while NPR and UPI attribute this claim to Trump. Al Jazeera and BBC attribute the claim to Trump as well, but BBC adds that Trump linked the decision to South Korea’s refusal to "give us a little hand" with Iran. Mother Jones and ABC News state that Trump cited his "very good relationship with Kim Jong Un" as a reason for reducing the drills, while NPR and UPI attribute this claim to Trump. Al Jazeera and BBC also attribute this claim to Trump, but BBC adds that Trump said Pyongyang had been "unthreatening and respectful" during his presidency. UPI and ABC News mention that Trump wrote on Truth Social that the drills "send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile" to North Korea, while Mother Jones and NPR attribute this statement to Trump. Al Jazeera and BBC also attribute this statement to Trump, but BBC adds that Trump said the drills were "costly" and "send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile" to North Korea.

Sources Mother Jones · NPR · Al Jazeera · ABC News · BBC · UPI

Prince Harry and Meghan leaving US for Britain after six-year royal feud

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are relocating from the United States to the United Kingdom later this month, according to multiple outlets. The couple, along with their two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, are expected to move to a private, non-royal residence outside London. The children are enrolled to start school in September. The move comes after a period of strained relations with the royal family, which began when the couple stepped down from their royal duties in 2020 and moved to California. The couple has not resumed their roles as working royals, and their status as private individuals remains unchanged.

The decision to return to the UK follows a meeting between Harry and King Charles III at Highgrove House in July, which marked the first time the king had seen his grandchildren in person in over four years. King Charles was reportedly informed of the couple’s plans on Sunday, and he has expressed willingness to see them in a private capacity. The move also comes after Harry expressed a desire for reconciliation with his family, particularly following his father’s diagnosis with an unspecified form of cancer.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Guardian both state that King Charles was informed of the couple’s decision on Sunday, while The Daily Wire and BBC report that the king was made aware of the plans on Sunday as well. The Guardian and The Daily Wire mention that the couple’s return was not discussed during their July visit to Highgrove, whereas The Washington Examiner and BBC suggest that the visit was a key development in their relationship. The Daily Wire and The Guardian note that Harry has remained estranged from his brother, Prince William, while The Washington Examiner and BBC do not explicitly state this. The Daily Wire includes a quote from GB News commentator Patrick Christys, which is absent from other accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · NPR · Just The News · BBC

Trump to tap Heidi Overton as FDA commissioner

President Trump has nominated White House aide Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration, according to multiple outlets. Overton, currently deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, was one of several candidates considered for the role. The nomination comes after former FDA commissioner Marty Makary resigned in May following clashes with the Trump administration over the safety of flavored vapes. Overton is expected to face Senate confirmation, with some senators expressing concerns about her qualifications and policies.

Overton has been involved in recent executive actions, including the signing of an order to reduce the number of childhood vaccines recommended for children and to split the MMR vaccine into separate shots. She has also been vocal about her opposition to abortion, describing it as "corrosive" to women and society. Her nomination has drawn criticism from Democrats and some Republicans, who argue that her policies could undermine public health and scientific integrity.

Where the accounts differ

Axios reports that Overton may not offer the reassurance the pharmaceutical industry was looking for and that industry analysts have criticized her nomination. The Guardian and FOX News attribute similar concerns to Overton's stance on abortion and vaccine policies. UPI and Washington Examiner note that Overton's nomination has caused tension within the MAHA movement, with some activists viewing her as too aligned with the traditional public health establishment. The Guardian and FOX News also highlight Overton's role in Trump's executive order on vaccines, which has been criticized by the American Academy of Pediatrics as "dangerous" and "disheartening."

Sources Axios · BBC · UPI · Washington Examiner · FOX News · The Guardian

Five Americans among seven killed in Kenya helicopter crash

A helicopter crash in northern Kenya killed seven people, including five Americans, according to multiple reports. The crash occurred on Wednesday morning while the aircraft was flying from the Loisaba Conservancy to the Ewaso Nyiro area in Samburu County. The Kenya Civil Aviation Authority confirmed the crash and stated an investigation was underway. The helicopter, owned by Lady Lori Helicopters, was operating a charter flight for the travel company &Beyond. The aircraft was a Eurocopter EC130 B4. Rescue and recovery efforts faced challenges due to difficult terrain and an active fire at the crash site.

The U.S. State Department confirmed that five of the deceased were American citizens, including a Florida-based Telemundo TV station manager and a Miami restaurateur. The State Department said it was in contact with local authorities and providing consular assistance. The identities of the victims were not immediately released, though some outlets reported that José Alberto Suárez, a Telemundo executive, and Ecuador's intelligence chief Michele Sensi-Contugi, along with his wife, were among those killed.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News and The Guardian both reported that five Americans were killed, including José Suárez and Roger Duarte. The Guardian also named Michele Sensi-Contugi and his wife, Stephany Holliham Yeaza, as victims. UPI and Just The News reported five Americans were killed but did not specify which individuals. FOX News and BBC also mentioned five Americans, but FOX News referred to José Suárez as a Telemundo executive, while CBS News and The Guardian provided more details about his role. The Guardian and BBC noted that Sensi-Contugi was visiting Kenya as a tourist, a detail not included in CBS News or UPI. The Guardian and BBC also mentioned the death of Sensi-Contugi's wife, while CBS News and UPI did not. The Guardian and BBC provided more context about the helicopter's route and the crash location, while UPI and Just The News omitted some details about the victims.

Sources CBS News · The Guardian · UPI · Just The News · BBC · FOX News

Graham says national security ‘not my thing’ but vows to back Trump’s defense agenda

Sen. Darline Graham Nordone (R-SC) admitted during a debate against Rep. Ralph Norman (R-SC) that she is not well-informed on national security, stating, “I’m not that informed on national security.” She defended President Donald Trump’s defense agenda, saying she supports the military and trusts Trump’s handling of the Iran situation. Graham, running to replace her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, also mentioned her brother’s influence on her views, stating she would follow his policies on defense. Norman, her opponent, argued that Trump’s approach to Taiwan and Iran demonstrates “peace through strength,” which deters antagonistic nations. He criticized Trump’s Iran policy, suggesting the president needs to better inform Americans about the situation.

Graham also faced criticism for misstating South Carolina’s population during the debate, claiming there are 50 million residents, while the actual population is approximately 5.5 million. Norman’s campaign pointed out the error on social media. The debate took place ahead of a Republican primary runoff on August 25, where Graham and Norman will face off for the GOP nomination in South Carolina’s special Senate election.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Daily Wire both report that Graham admitted to not being informed on national security, but The Daily Wire adds that former Gov. Nikki Haley criticized her for the remark. The Daily Caller and Associated Press describe the same admission, with The Daily Caller noting that Graham “faceplants” in the debate and misstates South Carolina’s population. The ABC News account includes audience boos during Graham’s response and mentions Haley’s criticism, while also noting that Graham later claimed South Carolinians care more about domestic issues than foreign policy. The Washington Examiner and The Daily Wire both mention Trump’s endorsement of Graham, while The Daily Caller and ABC News include details about Trump’s comments on other politicians.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller · Associated Press · ABC News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Disney, ABC file suit against Trump's FCC for retaliation against it

The Walt Disney Company and ABC have filed a lawsuit against the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), alleging the Trump administration is engaging in a retaliatory campaign against the network for its programming. The suit claims the FCC ordered an early license renewal for Disney’s eight owned-and-operated stations, which are not due for renewal until 2028. The lawsuit argues this action is an "existential threat" and part of a broader effort to punish ABC for its content. The suit was filed in a Washington, D.C., federal court, requesting an immediate block on FCC actions related to the early renewal process and a speedy hearing. The complaint also references President Trump’s social media posts criticizing ABC and its late-night programming, including a 2025 post where he suggested revoking broadcast licenses for networks that criticize him.

Where the accounts differ

UPI and The Daily Caller both mention Trump’s 2025 social media post about revoking licenses for networks that criticize him, while Straight Arrow News and Slate refer to a similar post from December 2025. The Daily Caller and The Daily Wire include details about FCC Chairman Brendan Carr’s investigation into Disney’s diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) practices, which UPI and NPR do not mention. The Daily Wire and Slate provide more context about the suspension of Jimmy Kimmel’s show in September 2025, which is omitted by UPI and The Daily Caller. Straight Arrow News and The Daily Wire both note that Carr launched an investigation into ABC’s DEI programs, while UPI and NPR do not specify the nature of the investigation.

Sources UPI · Straight Arrow News · The Daily Wire · Slate · NPR · The Daily Caller

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Boyfriend of Hayden Panettiere was at apartment when actor died

Hayden Panettiere’s on-and-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother, Zach Hickerson, were at the South Carolina apartment where the actor died over the weekend, according to a police report. The report states that a Greenville police officer met the brothers upon arrival and observed paramedics performing CPR on an unresponsive woman. The officer noted the patient did not appear to have any obvious physical reasons for being unresponsive. After attempts at lifesaving measures, Panettiere was declared dead at 2:31 p.m. No cause has been determined, and her death remains under investigation. An autopsy found no signs of trauma, and police said they saw no signs of foul play. Panettiere and Hickerson had a tumultuous relationship, with allegations of physical abuse. Hickerson was charged in 2020 with multiple counts of felony abuse and pleaded no contest to two counts of injuring a spouse or partner. He served a short time in jail and was sentenced to four years of probation and anger management. He recently asked a judge to reduce his conviction to misdemeanors, but the request was denied. Panettiere wrote about her decision to forgive Hickerson in her memoir.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and CBS News both state that Zach Hickerson identified Panettiere as his brother’s girlfriend, while The Daily Caller and Straight Arrow News do not mention this identification. The Guardian and CBS News note that Brian Hickerson showed the responding officer a bag of medication, while The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller do not mention this detail. The Guardian and CBS News report that the responding officer observed Zach Hickerson being very emotional while EMS worked on Panettiere, while The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller do not specify the emotional reactions of the brothers. The Guardian and CBS News mention that the police report is heavily redacted, while The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller do not mention redactions. The Guardian and CBS News report that the police report was obtained by CBS News, while The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller do not mention how the report was obtained.

Sources The Guardian · CBS News · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Russian missile barrage kills at least 13 people in Ukraine’s Kyiv, directly impacting civilian safety and escalating regional conflict.

Russian missile barrage kills at least 13 people in Ukraine’s Kyiv

Russian forces launched ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv, killing at least 13 people and wounding 33, according to Ukrainian officials. Explosions were reported across several districts, including Sviatoshynskyi, Solomianskyi, and Shevchenkivskyi, with a nine-storey residential building collapsing and catching fire in Solomianskyi. A children’s hospital in the district was also damaged. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that parts of the districts were without electricity and that people were trapped in another residential building. Ukraine’s Emergency Services confirmed at least 33 people were wounded in the attack. In the Brovary district of the Kyiv region, one person was killed and another wounded. Russia’s Ministry of Defence claimed it shot down 726 Ukrainian UAVs between Wednesday evening and Thursday morning.

The attacks prompted security responses in neighboring NATO countries, with Poland mobilizing aircraft and Romania scrambling jets after detecting aerial targets near the Ukrainian border. Ukraine’s new defence minister, Yevhenii Khmara, was confirmed by parliament, with Zelenskyy calling the appointment a sign of increased strength. Zelenskyy also appealed for more anti-ballistic missile support, citing a shortage of Patriot interceptors and the need for Ukraine’s FREYJA program to be operational by 2027.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and The Guardian both report that at least 13 people were killed, while ABC News and BBC report at least 12 and 13 respectively. Al Jazeera and The Guardian mention the collapse of a nine-storey residential building and damage to a children’s hospital in Solomianskyi, while ABC News and BBC do not specify which buildings were hit. ABC News and BBC report that Zelenskyy called the attack “massive” and described it as one of the most brutal, while Al Jazeera and The Guardian do not include this characterization. The Guardian and BBC mention the use of hypersonic missiles and specific types of Russian weaponry, which are not detailed in Al Jazeera or ABC News. ABC News and BBC report that Ukraine’s air force did not specify how many ballistic missiles were intercepted, while Al Jazeera and The Guardian do not mention this detail.

Sources Al Jazeera · ABC News · The Guardian · BBC

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

The brief ends here.

US, Canada hold last-minute talks to stop 50% U.S. tariffs

President Donald Trump announced a three-day pause on 50% tariffs on Canadian goods hours before they were set to take effect, citing a pending deal. The tariffs, which would have applied to $20 billion in Canadian imports, including liquor, dairy, and vehicles, were scheduled to begin at 12:01 a.m. on August 19. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney acknowledged the postponement but stated that work continued on reaching an agreement. The White House claimed the tariffs were imposed in response to Canada’s “discriminatory treatment” of U.S. commerce, while Canadian officials expressed concerns over U.S. tariffs on steel, aluminum, and softwood lumber. Both sides emphasized the importance of avoiding the tariffs, with U.S. trade officials noting the potential impact on American consumers and Canadian businesses.

The negotiations involved discussions over market access, economic security, and digital trade, with the U.S. seeking greater access to Canadian resources and Canada pushing for relief from existing tariffs. Trump also mentioned the potential revival of the Keystone XL Pipeline as part of the deal. Canadian officials, including Prime Minister Mark Carney, emphasized the need to build a “stronger, more competitive economy” while continuing to negotiate. The delay allowed for further talks, though no final agreement had been reached by the deadline.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News and UPI both mention the three-day pause on tariffs and Trump’s claim of a deal, but ABC includes details about the U.S. seeking military equipment and access to critical minerals, which UPI omits. UPI notes that Carney did not confirm a deal was reached, while ABC states that Carney said negotiations were “intense and delicate.” Fox Business and FOX News both report Trump’s mention of the Keystone XL Pipeline, but Fox Business attributes this to Trump’s social media post, while FOX News includes it in a quote from Trump. UPI and Washington Examiner both mention the postponement of tariffs until August 21, but UPI does not specify the three-day pause, while Washington Examiner notes the three-day delay. ABC and Fox Business both mention the impact on Canadian spirits, but Fox Business includes quotes from Chris Swonger, while ABC does not.

Sources ABC News · Slate · UPI · Washington Examiner · Fox Business · FOX News

Byron Donalds and David Jolly to face off in Florida governor's race

Florida voters cast their ballots in the primary elections on Tuesday, with Republican Rep. Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly emerging as the top contenders for governor. Donalds, backed by former President Donald Trump, won the Republican primary with 48.7% of the vote, defeating Lt. Gov. Jay Collins (24.8%) and far-right candidate James Fishback (10.5%). Jolly, a former Republican congressman who switched parties, secured 61.6% of the vote in the Democratic primary, defeating state lawmaker Dotie Joseph and criminal justice reform advocate Evelyn Castillo-Bach. The race for governor marks the first elections in Florida to use the new congressional districts signed into law in May, which were drawn by the state’s Republican-dominated legislature to favor right-wing candidates.

The race for governor is part of a broader trend of Florida shifting to the right, with Republicans dominating key statewide positions since 2019. Democrats, however, remain hopeful of making inroads, with Jolly seen as a potential candidate to attract more moderate voters. The state’s redistricting efforts, part of a national strategy under Trump to boost Republican chances in the midterms, have left Democrats struggling to win major statewide races.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and Washington Examiner both report that Donalds received Trump’s endorsement, while CBS News and Axios attribute the endorsement to Trump as well. However, Al Jazeera and Washington Examiner mention that DeSantis did not endorse any Republican candidate, while CBS News and Axios do not explicitly state this. The Washington Examiner provides specific vote percentages (48.7% for Donalds, 24.8% for Collins, 10.5% for Fishback), while Al Jazeera and CBS News do not include these figures. Axios and Washington Examiner note that Fishback made inflammatory comments, including calling Donalds a “Section 8 ghetto” and a “token black,” while Al Jazeera and CBS News do not mention these specific remarks.

Sources Al Jazeera · CBS News · Axios · BBC · Washington Examiner · New York Post

Florida Senate race set between Ashley Moody and Angie Nixon

In the Florida Senate primary, Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon defeated Republican candidate Alex Vindman, securing the Democratic nomination. Nixon, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, ran on progressive policies including Medicare for All, free childcare, and a national rent freeze. She will face off against Republican Sen. Ashley Moody in the November general election. Moody, appointed by Gov. Ron DeSantis to replace Marco Rubio, is backed by former President Donald Trump and has a history of supporting his agenda.

Nixon's victory was notable given her limited fundraising compared to Vindman, who raised over $16 million. Nixon's campaign focused on grassroots organizing and local support, particularly in Jacksonville and other parts of Florida. The race highlights the growing influence of progressive candidates within the Democratic Party, despite the state's traditionally Republican leanings.

Where the accounts differ

CBS News and Axios both report that Nixon defeated Vindman, but Axios notes that Nixon's win was a "stunning" upset due to her limited fundraising compared to Vindman's $16.3 million. CBS News does not mention the fundraising disparity. Straight Arrow News states that Vindman spent $850,000 on digital advertising in February, while Nixon's total campaign spending was over $700,000 by the end of last month. Washington Examiner and FOX News both mention Vindman's fundraising advantage, with FOX News citing FEC records showing Vindman reported $14.6 million in campaign receipts through June 30, more than 20 times Nixon's $625,000. Just The News does not provide specific figures on fundraising but notes Vindman's role in Trump's first impeachment.

Sources CBS News · Axios · Straight Arrow News · Washington Examiner · Just The News · FOX News

Lindsay Clancy had ‘thoughts of harming the children’, her mother testifies at trial

Lindsay Clancy’s mother, Paula Musgrove, testified in her daughter’s Massachusetts triple-murder trial that Clancy had told her she had thoughts of harming the children. Musgrove described her daughter’s deteriorating mental state in the months leading up to the killings, including text messages in which Clancy said she was “really sick” and “I don’t want to be alone.” Clancy’s defense is arguing that she suffered from postpartum psychosis and should not be held criminally responsible. The prosecution, however, claims she planned the murders and faked a suicide attempt. During the trial, a digital forensic expert testified that Clancy had searched for terms like “symptoms of postpartum psychosis” and “ketamine for suicidal ideation” in the weeks before the killings.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and CBS News both report that Musgrove testified Clancy told her she had thoughts of harming the children. However, CBS News includes a text message from Clancy to Musgrove in which she wrote, “I’m really sick. Something is wrong,” and that she had taken medication for anxiety, which she said made things worse. The Guardian does not include this specific text message. Additionally, CBS News notes that Musgrove said Clancy told her she was “doing better” in the days before the killings, while The Guardian does not mention this. UPI and The Daily Wire report that Clancy told a medical expert she heard a man’s voice telling her to kill the children and herself, but The Guardian and CBS News do not mention this claim. The Washington Examiner and FOX News report that Clancy told her husband she heard a voice telling her to kill the children and herself, but The Guardian and CBS News do not include this detail.

Sources The Guardian · CBS News · UPI · Washington Examiner · FOX News · The Daily Wire

Jon Ossoff denies 2028 presidential bid, faces backlash over Trump aide comments

Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) has denied any interest in running for president in 2028, stating he is focused on the 2026 midterm elections. Ossoff faced criticism after making remarks about President Donald Trump’s relationship with his aide Natalie Harp, which were interpreted as insinuating an inappropriate relationship. The comments sparked a strong reaction from the White House, with officials calling Ossoff a “cuck loser” and “cringeworthy, feminine theatre kid cosplaying as Barack Obama.” Ossoff also criticized Trump’s handling of the economy and the Iran war, accusing him of “lying” the country into conflict.

Ossoff’s remarks have drawn attention to the broader debate within the Democratic Party about how to approach the 2028 election. Some Democrats, including Ossoff and California Gov. Gavin Newsom, have adopted a more confrontational style, directly attacking Trump with personal jabs. Others, like Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, have advocated for a more measured, issue-focused approach. The controversy has also highlighted the media’s differing angles on the story, with some outlets emphasizing the personal nature of Ossoff’s comments and others focusing on the political implications.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and Axios both report that Ossoff denied any interest in a 2028 presidential bid, while The Daily Wire and The New York Post describe Ossoff as a potential 2028 candidate. The Washington Examiner and The New York Post attribute the claim that Ossoff has “zero interest” in 2028 to Ossoff himself, whereas Axios and The Daily Wire do not attribute this claim directly to Ossoff. The New York Post and The Daily Wire mention that Ossoff referred to Harp as “Natalie,” while The Washington Examiner and Axios do not specify the name used. The Daily Wire and The New York Post include quotes from Rep. Brandon Gill and environmental protection administrator Lee Zeldin criticizing Ossoff, which are absent in the Washington Examiner and Axios accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · New York Post · Axios · Straight Arrow News · The Dispatch · The Daily Wire

Rep. Cory Mills Loses Florida GOP Primary Amid Ethics Probe and Scandals

Rep. Cory Mills, a Republican congressman from Florida, lost his primary bid for re-election in the state's 7th Congressional District to Ryan Elijah, a former local TV news anchor. The race was marked by a series of allegations against Mills, including domestic abuse, campaign finance violations, and potential misconduct involving former partners. The House Ethics Committee has launched an investigation into these claims, which have also drawn scrutiny from the Department of Justice. Mills, who received the endorsement of President Donald Trump, faced significant opposition from within his own party, with several Florida Republicans endorsing Elijah instead. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis also distanced himself from Mills, stating he does not support him. Elijah's victory positions him to face Democratic nominee Bale Dalton in the general election, which Democrats view as a potential opportunity to flip the Republican-leaning district.

Mills' campaign has struggled with fundraising, with recent reports showing he raised only about $16,000 in July, compared to Elijah's over $186,000. The race has drawn attention due to the high-profile nature of Mills' controversies, which include allegations of domestic violence, stolen valor, and financial impropriety. Despite these issues, Mills' campaign highlighted his record of constituent services and efforts to evacuate Americans from conflict zones. The outcome of the primary has raised questions about the influence of Trump's endorsement and the role of ethics investigations in shaping congressional races.

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and The Daily Wire both report that Mills faced allegations of domestic abuse and that the House Ethics Committee is investigating him, but only The Daily Wire and CBS News mention that a former girlfriend accused Mills of threatening to release nude photos, leading to a restraining order. Mother Jones and CBS News also note that Mills' campaign raised only about $16,000 in July, while The Daily Wire states that the campaign has less than $70,000 in the bank. FOX News and Just The News do not mention the specific financial figures, while NPR and CBS News note that Elijah's campaign has over $186,000 in cash on hand. The Daily Wire and CBS News both mention that Mills is under investigation by the Department of Justice, while Mother Jones and FOX News report that Mills denied the existence of the DOJ probe. The Daily Wire and CBS News also state that Mills has denied all wrongdoing, while Mother Jones and NPR note that Mills has not been charged with any crime.

Sources Mother Jones · FOX News · The Daily Wire · CBS News · NPR · Just The News

No source labeled center covered this story.

Sen. Dan Sullivan and Mary Peltola Advance in Alaska Senate Primary

Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK) and former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-AK) advanced from Alaska’s nonpartisan primary, setting up a November general election race for the U.S. Senate. Sullivan, a veteran Republican and Trump ally, faces Peltola, the first Alaska Native to serve in Congress and a former House representative. The race is seen as a key contest for Democratic control of the Senate, with both candidates vying for a seat in a state that has traditionally favored Republicans. Peltola’s campaign recently distanced itself from an unsolicited endorsement from former Vice President Kamala Harris, who had previously supported her. The primary also featured another candidate named Dan Sullivan, a retired teacher, who was allowed to remain on the ballot after a judge rejected an effort to remove him. Alaska’s top-four primary system means the top four vote-getters advance to the general election, where ranked-choice voting will determine the winner.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire reports that Peltola’s campaign manager, Anton McParland, left the campaign just hours before the primary, citing a “Saturday Night Massacre” of staff firings. The Associated Press and Washington Examiner do not mention McParland’s departure, though the Examiner notes Peltola made staffing changes as she transitioned to the general election. The Daily Wire also claims Peltola rejected an unsolicited endorsement from Kamala Harris, while the Washington Examiner and Newsweek note that Peltola’s campaign dismissed an email from Harris’s PAC as unsolicited. The FOX News account states that Peltola was the only Democrat to win a statewide election in Alaska since 1972, a claim not made by other outlets. The NPR account does not mention the primary or the candidates, focusing instead on unrelated news.

Sources The Daily Wire · Associated Press · Washington Examiner · Newsweek · FOX News · NPR

No source labeled left covered this story.

Trump dismisses USS Lincoln criticism and snaps at CNN reporter to ‘be quiet’

President Donald Trump claimed he had third-hand reports that the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln was “beautifully maintained” despite extensive accounts of deteriorating living conditions during its lengthy deployment in the strait of Hormuz. At the White House on Monday, the president berated CNN reporter Kristen Holmes during a press availability, insisting she “be quiet” and describing the reporting as fake news. Trump also did not identify the “other people” he claimed had verified the anonymous admiral’s account. The Lincoln, a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier, left port from San Diego on 21 November 2025 and has now set a modern record for the longest time at sea without a port call. It has been more than 250 days since it has touched land. The Navy Times and Stars and Stripes have also largely confirmed reports of the Lincoln’s conditions, describing shortages of supplies and water and plumbing problems. Several sailors have attempted to leap from the ship according to their reports, prompting Democratic lawmakers to demand answers from the Pentagon.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that Trump did not identify the “other people” who verified the anonymous admiral’s account, while the Washington Examiner states that Trump told reporters last week that family members of the sailors on board are mistaken about the conditions and that the deployment has gone on “not nearly long enough.” The Nation claims that the Lincoln has been deployed in the Middle East since last November and has seen combat in the Iran War, while the BBC reports that the Lincoln has been deployed as part of the US-Iran war since 11 December. The Straight Arrow News states that Admiral Brad Cooper said problems involving food and hot water were reported months ago and have since been addressed by the ship’s leadership, while the Nation and the BBC report that the Navy denies a widespread mental health crisis on the Lincoln.

Sources The Guardian · The Nation · NPR · BBC · Straight Arrow News · Washington Examiner

No source labeled right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Mobile gold miners in eastern Congo complicate health workers’ efforts to contain Ebola, risking lives as the outbreak outpaces response efforts at unprecedented speed.

Mobile gold miners in eastern Congo complicate health workers’ efforts to contain Ebola

The Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo has reached 5,021 confirmed cases, including 2,378 deaths, according to government data. The Bundibugyo virus, which causes the current outbreak, has no approved vaccines or treatments. Health workers report that the outbreak is spreading faster than any previous Ebola outbreak in history, with cases increasing three times more rapidly than the 2014-2016 West Africa outbreak. The outbreak is concentrated in Ituri province, where artisanal gold mining is prevalent. Miners, including many children, work in hard-to-reach areas and often move between villages, complicating efforts to track and contain the virus. Health workers say that measures like handwashing and social distancing are not followed at mining sites, increasing the risk of transmission.

Miners and small-scale traders move frequently between mining areas and population centers, making it difficult to trace infected individuals and monitor the spread of the virus. Health workers have lost track of two miners who were identified as Ebola contacts after they moved to another mining site. Al Jazeera notes that the current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare form of Ebola first identified in Uganda in 2007, and that there are no licensed vaccines or specific approved therapies for it.
